questions.text: Define sigma-algebra. For rolling a die, Omega = {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Determine the sigma-algebra generated by {1}; another generated by {1} and {5}.
questions.originalText: Define σ-algebra. For rolling a die, Ω = {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Determine the σ-algebra generated by {1}; another generated by {1} and {5}; and by {1,5}. What questions can each address?

solution.hint: Start from {1} (or {1},{5}) and close under complement and union until nothing new appears.
solution.steps: $\sigma(\{1\})$: must contain $\{1\}$, its complement $\{2,3,4,5,6\}$, plus $\emptyset,\Omega$ — giving $\{\emptyset,\{1\},\{2,3,4,5,6\},\Omega\}$ (4 sets). This can answer exactly “was the outcome a 1?” $\sigma(\{1\},\{5\})$ (equivalently generated by $\{1,5\}$ together with $\{1\}$ separately) must additionally contain $\{5\}$, $\{2,3,4,6\}$, $\{1,5\}$, $\{2,3,4\}\cup\{6\}=\{2,3,4,6\}$ (already listed), and $\{1,5\}^c=\{2,3,4,6\}$: working through all unions/complements gives $\{\emptyset,\{1\},\{5\},\{1,5\},\{2,3,4,6\},\{2,3,4,5,6\},\{1,2,3,4,6\},\Omega\}$ (8 sets). This can answer “was it a 1?” and “was it a 5?” independently, but cannot distinguish e.g. $\{2\}$ from $\{3\}$.
solution.finalAnswer: σ({1}) has 4 sets; σ({1},{5}) has 8 sets, generated by closing under complements and unions.
solution.examReady: σ(\{1\})=\{∅,\{1\},\{1\}^c,\Omega\}; σ(\{1\},\{5\}) has $2^2=4$ atoms (\{1\},\{5\},\{2,3,4,6\}, plus their unions) giving $2^{\text{(number of atoms)}}=8$ sets total.
solution.commonMistakes: Forgetting to include $\emptyset$ and $\Omega$ explicitly, or stopping before closing under every pairwise union.

questions.text: Verify whether exp[B(t) - t/2] is a continuous-time martingale; derive its pdf, mean, and variance.
questions.originalText: Verify whether exp[B(t) − t/2] is a continuous-time martingale; derive its pdf, mean, and variance.

solution.hint: Use E[e^{\sigma B(t)}] = e^{\sigma^2 t/2} (the moment generating function of a normal random variable) to check the martingale property directly.
solution.steps: Let $M(t) = \exp[B(t)-t/2]$. **Mean:** since $B(t)\sim N(0,t)$, its MGF gives $\mathbb E[e^{B(t)}] = e^{t/2}$, so $\mathbb E[M(t)] = e^{-t/2}\cdot e^{t/2}=1$ for all $t$. **Martingale check:** for $s<t$, write $B(t)=B(s)+(B(t)-B(s))$ with the increment independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and $\sim N(0,t-s)$: $\mathbb E[M(t)\mid\mathcal F_s] = e^{-t/2}e^{B(s)}\,\mathbb E[e^{B(t)-B(s)}\mid\mathcal F_s] = e^{-t/2}e^{B(s)}\cdot e^{(t-s)/2} = e^{B(s)-s/2} = M(s)$. So $M(t)$ **is** a martingale. **Distribution:** $M(t)=e^{B(t)-t/2}$ is a log-normal random variable, since $B(t)-t/2 \sim N(-t/2, t)$; its pdf is the standard log-normal density with those parameters. **Variance:** using $\mathbb E[M(t)^2]=e^{-t}\mathbb E[e^{2B(t)}]=e^{-t}e^{2t}=e^{t}$, so $\operatorname{Var}(M(t)) = e^t - 1^2 = e^t-1$.
solution.finalAnswer: M(t) = exp[B(t) - t/2] IS a martingale; E[M(t)]=1, Var(M(t)) = e^t - 1, and M(t) is log-normally distributed.
solution.examReady: Martingale property follows from the MGF of the normal increment exactly cancelling the deterministic drift $-t/2$; this exponential-martingale construction is the prototype for geometric Brownian motion in finance.
solution.commonMistakes: Forgetting to condition on $\mathcal F_s$ when computing $\mathbb E[M(t)\mid\mathcal F_s]$ and instead just recomputing the unconditional mean — the martingale property is specifically about the conditional expectation.

questions.text: Define stopping time, with an example.
questions.originalText: Define predictable process and stopping time, with examples.

solution.finalAnswer: A random time τ is a stopping time (w.r.t. filtration {F_t}) if the event {τ ≤ t} is F_t-measurable for every t — i.e. you can tell, using only information available by time t, whether τ has already occurred. Example: the first time Brownian motion hits level 1, τ = inf{t : B(t)=1}, is a stopping time, since {τ≤t} depends only on the path up to time t.
